title: LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL

paper.title: LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL
paper.abstract:
Abstract While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions.
Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space.
However, naïvely optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic.
In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges.
We introduce LASER , a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time.
Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses
fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER .
Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/ .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn policies that improve upon the behavior policy using only a static dataset generated by that behavior policy, without further environment interaction [ 1 ] . This creates a central tension: improvement requires deviating from the behavior policy while choosing actions where the dataset provides reliable supervision. For a fixed state, actions outside the dataset support may receive spuriously high predicted values, which can be exploited by policy optimization to yield out-of-distribution (OOD) actions that perform poorly when deployed [ 1 ] . A major line of work regularizes a statistical distance between the learned and behavior policies to mitigate OOD actions [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, depending on the distance used, these methods can be either too restrictive and produce an overly conservative policy (e.g., KL divergence), or not restrictive enough and still produce OOD actions (e.g., Wasserstein distance, MMD distance) [ 7 ] . This has motivated a more direct alternative: enforce support constraints on the policy extraction process to guarantee that the actions produced lie within the support of the action distribution of the behavior policy [ 8 , 7 ] . In particular, these methods learn a flow-based generative model using flow matching [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] to imitate the behavior policy, resulting in a compact latent space that maps to the behavior policy. Assuming the decoder maps the latent prior’s support into the behavior policy’s support, any latent policy restricted to that support produces in-support actions, while allowing their probabilities to differ from those of the behavior policy. Policy optimization performed on this latent space, either via gradient descent (as in [ 7 ] ) or SAC [ 12 ] (as in [ 8 ] ), yields a policy that satisfies support constraints by construction. In this work, we argue that support constraints are only part of the story. Once policy optimization is restricted to the support, the central difficulty becomes policy extraction: how should one reliably select high-value actions from the support without collapsing to brittle modes or exploiting sharp artifacts of the learned critic? Even when actions remain in support, the critic may be sharp, irregular, or locally overestimated, and a low-entropy extraction procedure can collapse onto brittle modes. We study entropy regularization as an explicit objective for support-constrained flow policy optimization. While entropy regularization is well studied in online RL for its role in improving exploration [ 13 , 12 ] and robustness [ 13 , 14 ] , its role in offline RL, and in particular in support-constrained policy extraction, has not been isolated and made explicit. We argue that entropy regularization is also crucial in offline RL, not only in discouraging premature collapse of the policy to local minima, but also in smoothing the policy optimization landscape by regularizing the critic [ 15 ] . To this end, we propose L atent Space A djoint Matching for S upport-Constrained E ntropy- R egularized Offline RL ( LASER ), a framework for entropy-regularized support-constrained policy extraction with latent-space flow policies. LASER builds on the latent support parameterization used in recent flow-based offline RL methods [ 7 , 8 ] , but replaces implicit or architecture-dependent regularization with an explicit entropy-regularized policy improvement objective. The main technical challenge is that computing and optimizing the entropy of a flow policy in latent space is nontrivial. We address this using adjoint matching [ 16 ] , which enables entropy-regularized optimization of expressive flow policies in latent space while preserving the support constraints induced by the learned latent space. We make the following contributions: 1. We identify entropy regularization as a central ingredient for stable support-constrained policy extraction with flow-matching policies in offline RL. 2. We reinterpret recent support-constrained flow policy methods, including DSRL and ReFORM, through the lens of entropy regularization. 3. We introduce LASER , an algorithm for entropy-regularized offline policy improvement with latent-space flow policies that preserves dataset-support constraints while enabling smoother and more reliable policy extraction. 4. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LASER , using a fixed set of method-specific hyperparameters , achieves the strongest performance profiles among the evaluated flow-policy baselines.

Figure 1 : Both support constraints and entropy regularization are essential. Without support constraints, the policy generates OOD actions that have unreliable Q Q -values and thus fail. Without entropy regularization, the Q Q -function exhibits strange artifacts and the agents get stuck at the wall, resulting in failures on the left side. By combining support constraints and entropy regularization, LASER avoids OOD actions, regularizes the Q Q -function, and encourages policy exploration, resulting in a successful policy. Figure 2 : 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} -function and policy are poorly learned without entropy regularization. We plot the learned Q Q -functions (lighter colors denote higher value) at the state marked by the white circle in Figure 1 . Without entropy regularization, the policy becomes nearly deterministic and clusters at a false maximum which causes the agents to move up and get stuck at the wall ( Figure 1 ). Adding noise to the policy in TD learning (target policy smoothing [ 20 ] ) fixes the Q Q -function landscape, but the policy remains nearly deterministic and is suboptimal. sections.heading: 3.1 Entropy Regularization is Essential for Latent Space RL
sections.text:

However, we find this to be false. We illustrate this in a simple 2D reach-avoid environment (see Appendix E for details). (12) We discuss a more efficient method that does not require backpropagation through the flow map in the next subsection. Adding explicit entropy regularization improves both the Q Q -function and the policy ( Figure 2 ), resulting in a policy that successfully guides the agent around the wall to the target in the simple illustrative environment ( Figure 1 ). Remark 3.1 . Examining recent latent-space RL methods, we find that their policy extraction does include an entropy regularization term despite its importance not being made explicit in their papers. This is done either explicitly, as in DSRL [ 8 ] , which uses a Gaussian latent policy and an SAC-style objective [ 12 ] , or implicitly as in ReFORM [ 7 ] , where the geometric reflection term prevents latent collapse (see Section C.1 ). However, using an expressive flow policy for the latent-space policy and explicitly considering entropy regularization enables our method to empirically Pareto-dominate Gaussian policies ( Figure 3 ) and maximize the Q Q -function better than other implicit entropy regularization schemes ( Section C.1 ). A comparison of methods with no, implicit, and explicit entropy regularization across 20 tasks in more complex manipulation environments further supports the benefit of explicit regularization ( Section F.5 ). Figure 3 : Flow latent policy + adjoint matching Pareto-dominates a squashed Gaussian latent policy. For every entropy and Q Q -value achieved by the Gaussian latent policy, there exists an operating point achievable by the flow latent policy that has both higher entropy and higher Q Q -value. Why use a flow policy for π L \mathbf{\pi}_{	exttt{L}} ? While a Gaussian latent-space policy significantly simplifies entropy-regularized optimization, we motivate our use of a flow model with two arguments. (1) A Gaussian π L \pi_{	extsf{L}}{} produces unimodal latents, which restricts the ability of the full policy in action space to capture multimodality [ 7 ] . (2) While high-entropy policies facilitate robust Q Q -function learning and help avoid local minima, they often yield lower Q Q -values. By being more expressive, flow policies empirically Pareto-dominate Gaussian policies on the performance-entropy tradeoff ( Figure 3 ).

We now present L atent Space A djoint Matching for S upport-Constrained E ntropy- R egularized Offline RL ( LASER ). LASER combines the aforementioned insights to perform latent-space RL with an expressive flow decoder and efficient entropy-regularized policy optimization via adjoint matching. • Following [ 7 ] , we choose the latent prior q L = 𝒰 ⁡ ( ℬ l d ) q_{	extsf{L}}{}=\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{B}_{l}^{d}) to be the uniform distribution on the ball ℬ l d \mathcal{B}_{l}^{d} of radius l l in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , which has finite Lebesgue measure and satisfies the conditions of Lemma 3.2 . • Adjoint matching requires q L unif q_{	extsf{L}}^{\mathrm{unif}} , the uniform distribution over the support of q L q_{	extsf{L}}{} , to also be a flow model. While an analytical vector field can be derived since q L unif = q L q_{	extsf{L}}^{\mathrm{unif}}=q_{	extsf{L}}{} is the uniform distribution over the ball, it involves special functions with no easy closed-form expression (see Section C.2 ). Instead, we train a flow model via flow matching to match q L unif q_{	extsf{L}}^{\mathrm{unif}} with the same base distribution q B q_{	extsf{B}}{} as π L \pi_{	extsf{L}}{} to simplify the implementation. sections.heading: 4 Related Work
sections.text: We discuss the most closely related work in this section and defer a broader discussion of offline RL and generative policies to Appendix A . Distribution shift in offline RL. A central challenge in offline RL is distribution shift: learned value functions can overestimate actions outside the dataset support, causing policy improvement to select out-of-distribution actions with poor true value. Prior methods address this issue by regularizing the policy toward the behavior policy with statistical distances, learning pessimistic value functions, or explicitly restricting policy improvement to supported actions [ 5 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 4 ] . We follow the support-constrained perspective, using an expressive flow policy to enforce support by construction. Expressive generative policies for offline RL. Diffusion [ 27 , 28 ] and flow-matching [ 9 , 11 , 10 ] models have recently been used as expressive alternatives to deterministic or Gaussian policies, especially in robotic imitation learning where action distributions are often multimodal [ 29 , 30 ] . These policies have also been adapted to offline RL, where the goal is to improve beyond the behavior policy using a learned critic. Existing methods differ in how they use the critic: some use critic values to select, reweight, or clone high-value actions [ 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] , while others use critic gradients to directly improve the generated actions [ 35 , 30 , 21 ] . Most closely related to our optimization mechanism, [ 23 ] fine-tunes flow policies using critic gradients under a KL-regularized reward objective. Unlike these methods, which rely on statistical regularization to control distribution shift, LASER enforces support constraints through its latent action parameterization. Support-constrained policy extraction with latent-space RL. Recent methods avoid OOD actions by learning a latent action space whose decoder maps into the support of the behavior policy, then performing policy optimization in this latent space [ 19 , 8 , 7 ] . Our method builds on this idea, but revisits the optimization problem that remains once support has been controlled. In particular, we show that entropy regularization is important for preventing policy collapse and stabilizing policy extraction within the supported action set. Entropy regularization. Entropy regularization is a classical tool for smoothing policy optimization, improving robustness, and encouraging exploration [ 13 , 12 , 15 ] . In offline RL, though some works have noted its benefits for exploration during online fine-tuning [ 35 , 36 ] , it receives much less attention, perhaps due to the implicit entropy regularization effect from behavior policy regularization techniques. Our perspective is different: because support constraints are enforced by the policy parameterization, entropy regularization can be used for its standalone role in policy extraction.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We conduct experiments to answer the following research questions. (Q1): How does LASER perform against other offline RL algorithms with flow policies? (Q2): How sensitive is LASER to hyperparameters? (Q3): How does adjoint matching compare with BPTT? (Q4): Does the latent space decouple entropy regularization from behavior regularization? Details on implementation, baselines, environments, and additional results and ablations are in Appendix F .

sections.heading: 5.1 Setup
sections.text: Environments. We evaluate our method on the OGBench offline RL benchmark [ 18 ] . The main evaluation suite spans four environments, covering both locomotion and manipulation domains, with five tasks per environment. Each task is evaluated on two datasets ( clean and noisy ), yielding a total of 4 × 5 × 2 = 40 4\times 5\times 2=40 evaluation settings. We additionally evaluate harder tasks in Section F.5 . Baselines. Since recent studies have shown that flow-based policies outperform traditional alternatives [ 21 , 37 , 22 , 23 ] , we benchmark LASER against state-of-the-art flow-based methods. These include IFQL [ 32 , 21 ] , which combines a BC flow policy with an IQL critic and best-of- N N action selection; FQL [ 21 ] , which applies Wasserstein distance regularization; and QAM [ 23 ] , which uses adjoint matching to approximate the Q Q -value-weighted BC action distribution, alongside its extension QAM-E [ 23 ] that learns an additional residual policy. We also compare against latent-space RL methods, specifically DSRL [ 8 ] with a Gaussian latent policy, and ReFORM [ 7 ] with a reflected flow latent policy. The method-specific hyperparameters of LASER , ReFORM , and IFQL remain fixed across all evaluated tasks, while those of the other baselines vary by environment and dataset ( Table 3 ). All methods share the environment-dependent action chunk lengths and pessimistic backup weights ( Table 2 ).

sections.heading: 5.2 Results
sections.text: (Q1): LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance using a single set of method-specific hyperparameters. In Figure 5 , we present the performance profiles [ 38 ] aggregating the 40 main evaluation settings across both the clean and noisy datasets. The profiles show that LASER outperforms all evaluated baselines in aggregate. It achieves at least 95 % 95\% of the best mean success rate in 34 / 40 34/40 settings and a mean success rate of 100 % 100\% in 13 / 40 13/40 settings. A paired statistical comparison supports the aggregate advantage (global p = 1.35 × 10 − 3 p=1.35\times 10^{-3} ), with details in Section F.5 . Notably, on the noisy datasets, LASER and ReFORM achieve the highest mean success rates, underscoring the advantage of enforcing support constraints, which does not restrict policy improvement. Furthermore, LASER significantly improves upon ReFORM by using explicit entropy regularization and avoiding the static-flow behavior ( Sections C.1 and F.5 ). Figure 5 : Performance profile plots for the main evaluation suite with different datasets. For a given success rate τ \tau (x-axis), we plot the fraction of runs with a success rate ≥ τ \geq\tau [ 38 ] . Shading shows pointwise 95 % 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals, computed by resampling training seeds within each task 2000 times. LASER attains the strongest empirical performance profile on both datasets. Figure 6 : Ablation studies in cube-double-play-singletask-task2-v0 . Moderate values of the inverse temperature 1 / α ∈ [ 5 , 20 ] 1/\alpha\in[5,20] yield comparable results. Adjoint matching achieves better and more stable results than BPTT. Using a different q L q_{\textsf{L}}{} yields comparable final success rates in this task, consistent with the proposed separation between entropy regularization and behavior regularization. Lines show mean success rates, and shading spans the minimum and maximum across runs. (Q2): The key hyperparameter of LASER is the inverse temperature. Using a constant set of method-specific hyperparameters for LASER across all tasks demonstrates its robustness to different tasks and datasets. Nevertheless, we analyze the sensitivity of LASER to the inverse temperature 1 / α 1/\alpha ( Figure 6 ). Values of 1 / α ∈ [ 5 , 20 ] 1/\alpha\in[5,20] yield comparable results. At 1 / α = 3 1/\alpha=3 , performance drops on both datasets, whereas 1 / α = 30 1/\alpha=30 degrades performance on clean data but remains competitive on noisy data ( Table 6 ). We find that 1 / α = 10 1/\alpha=10 yields stable results for all environments. We also compare LASER with Q Q -only optimization and TPS in this ablation and find that LASER with 1 / α ∈ [ 5 , 20 ] 1/\alpha\in[5,20] outperforms both of them ( Table 6 ). In addition, we analyze sensitivity to σ 0 \sigma_{0} and find that LASER is robust to this hyperparameter ( Section F.5 ). (Q3): Adjoint matching achieves better results and is faster than BPTT using reparametrized gradients. A key advantage of adjoint matching is that it circumvents the need to perform BPTT on ( 12 ), which is computationally expensive and numerically unstable. We validate this empirically and observe that adjoint matching yields more stable training and stronger performance compared to BPTT ( Figure 6 ) while training 3.6 × 3.6\times faster ( 123 ​ it / s 123\,\mathrm{it/s} vs 34 ​ it / s 34\,\mathrm{it/s} ). (Q4): The latent space successfully decouples entropy regularization from behavior regularization. To understand the improvements of LASER , we change q L q_{\textsf{L}}{} to a distribution with the same support but a different density, which changes the behavior regularization effect but keeps the same latent-space entropy regularization (see Section F.5 ). Both runs retain the uniform entropy reference on the same latent ball. Changing the decoder prior can still alter the learned latent-to-action mapping and learning dynamics, while leaving the entropy regularizer unchanged. We observe that changing the decoder prior yields comparable final success rates in this task, consistent with the proposed separation between latent-space entropy regularization and behavior regularization ( Figure 6 ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced LASER , an entropy-regularized approach to support-constrained flow policy optimization for offline RL. Our key insight is that support constraints and entropy regularization solve different problems: the former prevent OOD actions, while the latter stabilizes policy extraction within the learned dataset support. By combining a flow-based decoder with latent-space adjoint matching, LASER effectively helps prevent mode collapse, smooths the optimization landscape, and avoids local minima, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on the OGBench suite with fixed method-specific hyperparameters. Limitations and Future Work. We identify several promising avenues for extension. First, although adjoint matching circumvents the need for BPTT, solving the ODEs needed to sample from the flow model during training remains computationally intensive for deep neural ODEs. This computational cost could be reduced through distillation [ 22 ] . Second, by relying on the decoder to enforce support constraints, LASER inherits OOD errors made by the decoder itself. Integrating behavior cloning methods with stricter support constraints, diagnosing when the BC model generates OOD errors, or applying a pre-trained robust BC model could mitigate this. In addition, LASER uses a simple value-function learning method and an actor-critic architecture similar to those in [ 21 ] . Both could be improved using ideas from [ 39 , 40 , 41 , 37 ] . Broader Impacts. Learning policies from existing datasets may reduce the cost and risks of online data collection in robotics. However, support constraints alone do not guarantee safe behavior, as datasets may contain unsafe actions and learned decoders can make errors. Deployment under distribution shift could therefore cause physical harm. Safety validation and monitoring remain necessary before deploying these policies on physical systems.

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended Related Work
sections.text: Mitigating distribution shift in offline RL. A central challenge in offline RL is mitigating distribution shift: learned value functions can overestimate actions that are not in the dataset, causing the policy to select these out-of-distribution actions. Classical approaches address this issue by either regularizing the policy to remain close to the behavior policy with statistical distances (e.g., KL divergence [ 2 , 3 , 6 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 , 25 ] , MMD distance [ 5 ] or Wasserstein distance [ 6 ] ), or regularizing the value function to be pessimistic on out-of-distribution actions [ 24 , 25 , 46 , 39 , 47 , 48 ] . Another family of methods addresses the OOD problem by penalizing actions that fall outside the support of the behavior policy [ 5 , 26 , 4 , 49 ] . However, these methods rely on heuristic sample-based proxies [ 5 ] or Gaussian density approximations [ 26 , 4 , 49 ] which can fail to capture expressive multimodal behavior policies. Expressive generative policies for offline RL. Diffusion [ 27 , 28 ] and flow-matching [ 9 , 11 , 10 ] models have recently been used as expressive alternatives to deterministic or Gaussian policies, especially in robotic imitation learning where action distributions are often multimodal [ 29 , 50 , 51 , 30 ] . These policies have also been adapted to offline RL, where the goal is to improve beyond the behavior policy using a learned critic. However, because flow and diffusion policies generate actions through an iterative sampling process, critic-based optimization is more challenging than for standard Gaussian actors. Existing reward-optimization methods for generative policies can be broadly divided by how they use the learned critic: critic-evaluation methods , which use only scalar values Q ⁡ ( s , a ) Q(s,a) to select or reweight actions, and critic-gradient methods , which use ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a ) \nabla_{a}Q(s,a) to directly improve generated actions. (i) Critic-evaluation methods include sampling-based methods that imitate the behavior policy and use the critic to sample from the reward-tilted distribution either at test time [ 31 , 32 ] or during training, when the sampled actions serve as imitation targets [ 52 ] . These methods often reliably improve the quality of the extracted policy at greater computational cost and depend on the quality of the behavior policy. Weighted behavioral cloning methods also fall under this category. These methods use the critic to assign per-sample weights in the diffusion or flow-matching loss, selectively cloning high-value actions in the dataset [ 33 , 35 , 34 ] , but generally do not optimize the learned policy towards the reward-tilted distribution [ 23 ] . (ii) Some critic-gradient methods combine a behavior-cloning term with a term that increases the critic-estimated value. These methods require backpropagation through the iterative sampling process [ 30 , 53 , 54 , 55 ] , which can be computationally expensive and unstable [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] . Other methods learn a distilled policy [ 21 , 56 , 57 , 58 , 59 ] at the expense of policy expressiveness. Another line of work uses guidance [ 60 , 61 ] during the iterative sampling process to favor high-value actions [ 62 , 63 , 64 ] , but these methods rely on approximations that do not have theoretical guarantees [ 65 , 23 ] . Most closely related to our optimization mechanism, [ 23 ] provides an efficient way to fine-tune flow-based policies using critic gradients and a KL-regularized reward objective via adjoint matching [ 16 ] . However, unlike critic-evaluation methods where samples from the learned policy are either directly cloned (sampling-based methods) or selectively cloned (weighted BC methods), these methods rely on statistical distance regularization to avoid the OOD problem (e.g., L2 / Wasserstein distance [ 21 ] or KL regularization [ 23 ] ). A key challenge is that the regularization weight is a hyperparameter that significantly affects the performance and needs to be tuned for each task and dataset [ 18 , 21 ] . Our method falls under the critic-gradient category as we also use adjoint matching to optimize the policy with critic gradients under KL regularization. However, to address the OOD problem, LASER relies on the latent space to enforce the support constraints by construction instead of using KL regularization toward the behavior policy, as in [ 23 ] , which can be too restrictive in cases where optimal actions have very low probability under the behavior policy [ 5 ] . Support constraints in offline RL. Instead of addressing the OOD problem with regularization, another line of work proposes to address the OOD problem by learning a bounded latent space that maps to the support of the behavior policy, then performing policy extraction in this latent space to restrict the support of the learned policy by construction [ 19 , 8 , 7 ] . Our work follows this support-constrained perspective, but revisits the optimization problem that remains after support has been controlled. Namely, we find that entropy regularization is essential to prevent policy collapse, and leverage adjoint matching [ 16 ] to perform entropy-regularized policy extraction in latent space with an expressive flow policy that achieves a better performance-entropy tradeoff than Gaussian policies. Entropy-regularized policy extraction. The role of entropy regularization has been well identified in online RL as a way to improve exploration [ 13 , 12 ] and policy robustness [ 13 , 14 ] and to smooth the optimization landscape [ 15 ] . In offline RL, while some works note the benefits of entropy regularization for exploration [ 35 , 36 ] , the importance of entropy regularization has been less emphasized, perhaps due to the implicit entropy regularization effect from various behavior policy regularization techniques. In our setting, the learned decoder and latent support constraint handle support control, so no separate behavior-policy regularization term is needed. This makes the role of entropy regularization in policy extraction explicit.

To illustrate this phenomenon, we train ReFORM on the 2D toy environment introduced in Figure 3 . The learned latent distribution and its resulting action distribution are visualized in Figure 7 . We empirically observe that the latent mass inappropriately concentrates along two radii, resulting in a suboptimal action distribution. We also conduct additional experiments in cube-double in Section F.5 to measure how often the boundary correction is activated. Interestingly, we find that this static flow artifact unintentionally serves as an implicit entropy regularizer, which partially explains ReFORM’s empirical success. sections.heading: Critic Learning.
sections.text: The critic is learned via the standard TD learning objective ( 2 ) with an ensemble of K K critics. In some environments, we found that using a pessimistic target-value backup [ 66 ] can improve performance. In that case, the loss function becomes L ( ϕ j ) = 𝔼 ( s , a , s ′ ) ∼ 𝒟 , a ′ ∼ π A ( ⋅ | s ′ ) [ ( Q ϕ j ( s , a ) − r − γ ( Q ϕ ^ mean ( s ′ , a ′ ) − ρ Q ϕ ^ std ( s ′ , a ′ ) ) ) 2 ] , L(\phi_{j})=\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{D},a^{\prime}\sim\pi_{\textsf{A}}(\cdot|s^{\prime})}\left[\left(Q_{\phi_{j}}(s,a)-r-\gamma\left(Q_{\hat{\phi}}^{\mathrm{mean}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-\rho Q_{\hat{\phi}}^{\mathrm{std}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right)\right)^{2}\right], (48) where ϕ j \phi_{j} denotes the parameters of the j j th critic, Q ϕ ^ mean ​ ( s ′ , a ′ ) ≔ 1 K ​ ∑ k Q ϕ ^ k ​ ( s ′ , a ′ ) Q_{\hat{\phi}}^{\mathrm{mean}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\coloneqq\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}Q_{\hat{\phi}_{k}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}) , Q ϕ ^ std ​ ( s ′ , a ′ ) = 1 K ​ ∑ k ( Q ϕ ^ k ​ ( s ′ , a ′ ) − Q ϕ ^ mean ​ ( s ′ , a ′ ) ) 2 Q_{\hat{\phi}}^{\mathrm{std}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})=\sqrt{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k}\left(Q_{\hat{\phi}_{k}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})-Q_{\hat{\phi}}^{\mathrm{mean}}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime})\right)^{2}} , and ρ \rho is the pessimistic backup weight.

Projection enforces latent support, but if it places positive probability on the boundary, the resulting law has a singular component and no Lebesgue density. Thus, the entropy identity ( 12 ) and the optimality characterization in Lemma 3.2 do not directly apply to this projected law. The projected implementation is a practical approximation to the density-based formulation.

sections.heading: Appendix E Details of the Reach-avoid Example in Figure 1
sections.text: The agent starts in one of two regions at the bottom and must reach the goal at the top. Actions are two-dimensional velocities. If a proposed next state lies inside an obstacle, we set s ′ = s s^{\prime}=s . The “No Entropy Regularization” baseline is constructed by replacing the adjoint matching component in LASER with plain gradient ascent, and the generated latent samples z z are squashed inside the ball ℬ l d \mathcal{B}_{l}^{d} to satisfy the support constraint. The “No Support Constraint” baseline is constructed with a QAM [ 23 ] model with a large inverse temperature τ \tau that drives the action distribution away from the behavior policy distribution.

sections.heading: F.1 Environments
sections.text: We conduct experiments on the widely used OGBench offline RL benchmark [ 18 ] . Although OGBench is designed for offline goal-conditioned RL, it provides the -singletask flag for standard offline RL. We use 4 environments in the main comparison, including one locomotion environment ( antmaze ) and three manipulation environments ( cube-single , cube-double , and scene ), each with 5 tasks. For each task, we consider 2 datasets, yielding a total of 40 tasks. We consider the following tasks with clean datasets, i.e., the demonstrations are randomly generated by an expert policy: • antmaze-large-navigate-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 • cube-single-play-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 • cube-double-play-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 • scene-play-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 In addition, we consider the following tasks with noisy datasets, i.e., the demonstrations are generated by a highly noisy policy: • antmaze-large-explore-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 • cube-single-noisy-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 • cube-double-noisy-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 • scene-noisy-singletask-task{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}-v0 More details of the environments and datasets can be found in [ 18 ] .

sections.heading: DSRL .
sections.text: DSRL [ 8 ] is a recently proposed latent-space RL algorithm, which has several key differences compared with LASER . First, the latent distribution of the decoder is a standard Gaussian in DSRL , i.e., q L = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) q_{\textsf{L}}{}=\mathcal{N}(0,I) . Because the support of q L q_{\textsf{L}}{} is unbounded, steering q L q_{\textsf{L}}{} might generate a distribution that has high density far from the origin, where the samples are not well represented during the training of the decoder. To avoid this problem, DSRL parameterizes the latent policy π L \pi_{\textsf{L}}{} with a squashed Gaussian distribution that only generates samples within the range of [ − σ z , σ z ] [-\sigma_{z},\sigma_{z}] , where σ z \sigma_{z} is a hyperparameter that requires fine-tuning for each task. DSRL follows an SAC-style loss [ 12 ] and explicitly regularizes the entropy, which is straightforward for a Gaussian latent policy. However, because of the Gaussian parameterization, DSRL has a suboptimal entropy-performance tradeoff as shown in Figure 3 .

sections.heading: F.3 Hyperparameters
sections.text: We organize the hyperparameters into three distinct categories. Fixed common hyperparameters ( Table 1 ) are shared across all algorithms and remain constant across all tasks. We do not fine-tune these, but instead adopt the standard values established in prior work [ 21 , 23 , 7 ] . Environment-specific common hyperparameters ( Table 2 ) are also shared across algorithms but vary by environment and dataset to optimize baseline performance. Following [ 23 ] , we perform a minimal sweep over two candidate values for these settings: 1 or 5 for the action chunking length, and 0 or 0.5 for the pessimistic backup weight. Environment-specific unique hyperparameters ( Table 3 ) are specific to individual baselines (namely FQL , DSRL , QAM , and QAM-E ) and require per-environment tuning. For these, we rely on the optimal values reported in their respective papers or tune them empirically. One notable exception is the edit scale σ a \sigma_{a} for QAM-E . While the original authors sometimes set σ a = 0 \sigma_{a}=0 [ 23 ] , making QAM-E identical to QAM , we enforce a minimum value of σ a = 0.01 \sigma_{a}=0.01 to ensure the algorithms remain distinct. Finally, while LASER introduces two unique hyperparameters, we keep them strictly fixed across all tasks. Specifically, we set 1 / α = 10 1/\alpha=10 and choose σ 0 \sigma_{0} such that Pr w ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 0 2 ​ I ) ​ ( ‖ w ‖ ≤ l ) = 0.999 \mathrm{Pr}_{w\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}I)}(\|w\|\leq l)=0.999 . sections.heading: Ablation study of entropy regularization.
sections.text: To test the efficacy of entropy regularization beyond the simple environment introduced in Section 3.1 , we extend the entropy regularization comparison to cube-single and cube-double environments with both clean and noisy datasets. NoER uses the same latent support constraint, network architectures, critic design, and other training settings as LASER , but directly maximizes Q Q through the latent flow using reparametrized gradients without entropy regularization. ReFORM instead uses a reflected flow with implicit entropy regularization ( Section C.1 ), while LASER optimizes an explicitly entropy-regularized objective via adjoint matching. Table 5 reports the results for all five tasks in each environment with both clean and noisy datasets. We observe that both implicit ( ReFORM ) and explicit ( LASER ) entropy regularization help and significantly improve on NoER , and explicit entropy regularization ( LASER ) performs better than implicit entropy regularization ( ReFORM ). sections.heading: Inverse temperature and target policy smoothing.
sections.text: We compare Q Q -only latent optimization ( NoER ), target policy smoothing ( TPS ), and LASER with different inverse temperatures on cube-double task 2 using both clean and noisy datasets. TPS [ 20 ] augments NoER by adding independent zero-mean Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.2 0.2 , clipped to [ − 0.5 , 0.5 ] [-0.5,0.5] , to the target actions in the critic update. The perturbed actions are then clipped to the action bounds. As shown in Table 6 , our default 1 / α = 10 1/\alpha=10 outperforms both NoER and TPS on both datasets. Strong regularization ( 1 / α = 3 1/\alpha=3 ) reduces performance on both datasets, whereas weak regularization ( 1 / α = 30 1/\alpha=30 ) performs poorly on the clean dataset but remains competitive on the noisy dataset. One possible explanation is that noisy demonstrations provide broader action coverage, reducing critic artifacts. sections.heading: Uniform-mixture ablation in action space.
sections.text: LASER combines entropy optimization with bounded latent support. To examine a simple alternative in action space, we evaluate QAM+Mix , which broadens QAM’s reference toward a uniform distribution over the action space. With probability η \eta , each behavior-cloning target is replaced by an action sampled uniformly within 𝒜 \mathcal{A} . Adjoint matching then uses the reference flow learned from these modified targets. In the ideal KL-regularized formulation, η = 0 \eta=0 recovers QAM, while η = 1 \eta=1 yields action-space maximum-entropy optimization. Thus, η \eta controls how strongly the reference distribution is broadened toward uniform. On cube-double-play-singletask-task2-v0 with the clean dataset, both tested mixing probabilities ( η = 0.03 \eta=0.03 and η = 0.1 \eta=0.1 ) reduce QAM ’s mean success rate ( Table 7 ). The results show that this naïve approach does not perform well. Table 7 : Uniform-mixture ablation in action space on cube-double task 2 with the clean dataset. sections.heading: Ablation study of the gradient clipping technique.
sections.text: A known drawback of adjoint matching is its tendency to produce large gradients, which can destabilize the training process [ 16 , 23 ] . In Figure 8 , we compare three variants on cube-double task 2 with clean data: terminal-gradient clipping disabled with a parameter-gradient cap of 10, disabled with a cap of 1, and enabled with a cap of 10 (our default). Both enabling terminal-gradient clipping and reducing the parameter-gradient cap improve stability over the first variant, with comparable performance.

sections.heading: Detailed results.
sections.text: The full results for each algorithm on the 40 main evaluation settings are provided in Table 11 . Success rates are bolded for algorithms achieving at least 95 % 95\% of the best performance per task. For every method and seed, we evaluate the final checkpoint. The main-suite training budgets are 5 million updates for antmaze-large-navigate , 8 million for antmaze-large-explore , 1 million for cube-single-noisy , and 2 million for the remaining settings. The training budgets are selected such that all methods converge. Each checkpoint is evaluated over 50 episodes, and we report the mean and standard deviation across 3 seeds. We observe that LASER yields the best overall performance, achieving near-perfect success rates on multiple tasks.

sections.heading: Statistical comparison.
sections.text: We pair results across the 40 main task–dataset settings, averaging each method’s success rate over its 3 seeds before comparison. For each baseline j j , a one-sided paired t t -test evaluates H 0 , j : Δ j ≤ 0 H_{0,j}:\Delta_{j}\leq 0 , where Δ j \Delta_{j} denotes the expected difference between LASER ’s and baseline j j ’s setting-level mean success rates. To test for improvement over every baseline, we use an intersection–union test of H 0 : ⋃ j { Δ j ≤ 0 } H_{0}:\bigcup_{j}\{\Delta_{j}\leq 0\} against H 1 : Δ j > 0 H_{1}:\Delta_{j}>0 for all j j . The global p p -value is max j ⁡ p j = 1.35 × 10 − 3 \max_{j}p_{j}=1.35\times 10^{-3} ( Table 10 ), rejecting H 0 H_{0} at the 0.05 0.05 level under the paired-test assumptions. This inference treats setting-level differences as independent despite shared environments and datasets, so we interpret it as supporting evidence for aggregate performance on this suite. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.08989v1 [cs.LG] 06 Oct 2026 LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL Songyuan Zhang Affiliation: MIT Email: szhang21@mit.edu Oswin So Affiliation: MIT Email: oswinso@mit.edu Eric Yang Yu Affiliation: MIT Email: eyyu@mit.edu Matthew Cleaveland Affiliation: MIT Lincoln Laboratory Email: chuchu@mit.edu Peter Crowley-Dolen Affiliation: MIT Lincoln Laboratory Email: matthew.cleaveland@ll.mit.edu Chuchu Fan Affiliation: MIT Email: Peter.Crowley-Dolen@ll.mit.edu Abstract While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space. However, naïvely optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic. In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges. We introduce LASER , a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time. Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER . Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/ . 0 0 footnotetext: DISTRIBUTION STATEMENT A. Approved for public release. Distribution is unlimited. 1 Introduction Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn policies that improve upon the behavior policy using only a static dataset generated by that behavior policy, without further environment interaction [ 1 ] . This creates a central tension: improvement requires deviating from the behavior policy while choosing actions where the dataset provides reliable supervision. For a fixed state, actions outside the dataset support may receive spuriously high predicted values, which can be exploited by policy optimization to yield out-of-distribution (OOD) actions that perform poorly when deployed [ 1 ] . A major line of work regularizes a statistical distance between the learned and behavior policies to mitigate OOD actions [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, depending on the distance used, these methods can be either too restrictive and produce an overly conservative policy (e.g., KL divergence), or not restrictive enough and still produce OOD actions (e.g., Wasserstein distance, MMD distance) [ 7 ] . This has motivated a more direct alternative: enforce support constraints on the policy extraction process to guarantee that the actions produced lie within the support of the action distribution of the behavior policy [ 8 , 7 ] . In particular, these methods learn a flow-based generative model using flow matching [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] to imitate the behavior policy, resulting in a compact latent space that maps to the behavior policy. Assuming the decoder maps the latent prior’s support into the behavior policy’s support, any latent policy restricted to that support produces in-support actions, while allowing their probabilities to differ from those of the behavior policy. Policy optimization performed on this latent space, either via gradient descent (as in [ 7 ] ) or SAC [ 12 ] (as in [ 8 ] ), yields a policy that satisfies support constraints by construction. In this work, we argue that support constraints are only part of the story. Once policy optimization is restricted to the support, the central difficulty becomes policy extraction: how should one reliably select high-value actions from the support without collapsing to brittle modes or exploiting sharp artifacts of the learned critic? Even when actions remain in support, the critic may be sharp, irregular, or locally overestimated, and a low-entropy extraction procedure can collapse onto brittle modes. We study entropy regularization as an explicit objective for support-constrained flow policy optimization. While entropy regularization is well studied in online RL for its role in improving exploration [ 13 , 12 ] and robustness [ 13 , 14 ] , its role in offline RL, and in particular in support-constrained policy extraction, has not been isolated and made explicit. We argue that entropy regularization is also crucial in offline RL, not only in discouraging premature collapse of the policy to local minima, but also in smoothing the policy optimization landscape by regularizing the critic [ 15 ] . To this end, we propose L atent Space A djoint Matching for S upport-Constrained E ntropy- R egularized Offline RL ( LASER ), a framework for entropy-regularized support-constrained policy extraction with latent-space flow policies. LASER builds on the latent support parameterization used in recent flow-based offline RL methods [ 7 , 8 ] , but replaces implicit or architecture-dependent regularization with an explicit entropy-regularized policy improvement objective. The main technical challenge is that computing and optimizing the entropy of a flow policy in latent space is nontrivial. We address this using adjoint matching [ 16 ] , which enables entropy-regularized optimization of expressive flow policies in latent space while preserving the support constraints induced by the learned latent space. We make the following contributions: 1. We identify entropy regularization as a central ingredient for stable support-constrained policy extraction with flow-matching policies in offline RL. 2. We reinterpret recent support-constrained flow policy methods, including DSRL and ReFORM, through the lens of entropy regularization. 3. We introduce LASER , an algorithm for entropy-regularized offline policy improvement with latent-space flow policies that preserves dataset-support constraints while enabling smoother and more reliable policy extraction. 4. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LASER , using a fixed set of method-specific hyperparameters , achieves the strongest performance profiles among the evaluated flow-policy baselines. 2 Preliminaries 2.1 Offline RL We use Δ ⁡ ( 𝒳 ) \Delta(\mathcal{X}) to denote the set of probability distributions over 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , and gray notation for placeholder variables. Figure 1 : Both support constraints and entropy regularization are essential. Without support constraints, the policy generates OOD actions that have unreliable Q Q -values and thus fail. Without entropy regularization, the Q Q -function exhibits strange artifacts and the agents get stuck at the wall, resulting in failures on the left side. By combining support constraints and entropy regularization, LASER avoids OOD actions, regularizes the Q Q -function, and encourages policy exploration, resulting in a successful policy. Figure 2 : 𝐐 \mathbf{Q} -function and policy are poorly learned without entropy regularization. We plot the learned Q Q -functions (lighter colors denote higher value) at the state marked by the white circle in Figure 1 . Without entropy regularization, the policy becomes nearly deterministic and clusters at a false maximum which causes the agents to move up and get stuck at the wall ( Figure 1 ). Adding noise to the policy in TD learning (target policy smoothing [ 20 ] ) fixes the Q Q -function landscape, but the policy remains nearly deterministic and is suboptimal. With entropy regularization, the policy samples spread out more and yield a better regularized Q Q -function, enabling the agents to move around the wall and reach the target ( Figure 1 ).
